items.new: It seemed that rather late on the previous afternoon, three of the stranger's boats had been engaged with a shoal of whales that had led them some four or five miles from the ship; and while they were still in swift chase to windward, the white hump and head of Moby Dick had suddenly loomed up out of the water, not very far to leeward. At that, the fourth rigged boat — a reserve one — had been instantly lowered to give chase. After a keen sail before the wind, this fourth boat — the swiftest-keeled of all — seemed to have succeeded in fastening to him; at least, as far as the man at the mast-head could tell anything about it. In the distance he saw the boat shrunk to a dot; then a swift gleam of bubbling white water; and after that, nothing more. From this it was concluded that the stricken whale must have run away with his pursuers for some indefinite distance, as often happens. There was some apprehension, but as yet no real alarm. The recall signals were hoisted in the rigging; darkness came on; and since the ship had to pick up her three boats far to windward before going in search of the fourth in exactly the opposite direction, she had not only been forced to leave that boat to its fate until nearly midnight, but for the time being to increase her distance from it. But once the rest of her crew were at last safe aboard, she crowded on all sail — studding-sail on studding-sail — after the missing boat, lighting a fire in her try-pots as a beacon, with every other man aloft on the lookout. But though she then sailed far enough to reach the presumed spot where the missing men were last seen; though she then stopped to lower her spare boats to row all around her; and, finding nothing, had dashed on again, stopped again, and lowered her boats again; and though she had kept doing this until daylight — still not the least glimpse of the missing keel had been seen.

This is because, in such a wilderness of running rigging, whose various relations aloft cannot always be told with certainty from what can be seen of them on deck, and when the deck-ends of these ropes are being cast off from their fastenings every few minutes, it would be only a natural fatality if, without a constant watchman, the hoisted sailor were cast adrift through some carelessness of the crew and fell swooping down into the sea. So Ahab's proceedings in this matter were not unusual. The only strange thing about them seemed to be that Starbuck — almost the only man who had ever ventured to oppose him with anything even slightly approaching decisiveness, and one of those, too, whose faithfulness on the lookout he had seemed somewhat to doubt — it was strange that this was the very man he should choose as his watchman, freely placing his whole life in the hands of a man he otherwise distrusted.

For forty years Ahab has forsaken the peaceful land, for forty years to make war on the horrors of the deep! Aye and yes, Starbuck, out of those forty years I have not spent three ashore. Guinea-coast slavery of solitary command! — when I think of all this, only half-suspected, not so keenly known to me before — and how for forty years I have fed on dry salted fare, fit emblem of the dry nourishment of my soil! — while the poorest landsman has had fresh fruit to his daily hand, and broken the world's fresh bread against my moldy crusts — away, whole oceans away, from that young girl-wife I married when I was past fifty, and sailed for Cape Horn the next day, leaving only one dent in my marriage pillow — wife? wife? — rather a widow with her husband alive! Aye, I widowed that poor girl when I married her, Starbuck; and then the madness, the frenzy, the boiling blood and the smoking brow with which, for a thousand lowerings, old Ahab has furiously, foamingly chased his prey — more a demon than a man! — aye, aye! what a forty years' fool — fool — old fool, old Ahab has been! Why this strife of the chase? Why weary and palsy the arm at the oar, and the iron, and the lance? How is Ahab the richer or better now? Look. Oh, Starbuck! is it not hard that, with this weary load I bear, one poor leg should have been snatched from under me? Here, brush this old hair aside; it blinds me, so that I seem to weep. Locks so gray never grew except out of some ashes! But do I look very old, so very, very old, Starbuck? I feel deadly faint, bowed and humped, as though I were Adam, staggering beneath the piled-up centuries since Paradise. God! God! God! — crack my heart! — stave in my brain! — mockery! mockery! bitter, biting mockery of gray hairs, have I lived enough joy to wear you, and to seem and feel so intolerably old? Close! stand close to me, Starbuck; let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God. By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone! this is the magic glass, man; I see my wife and my child in your eye. No, no; stay on board, on board! — do not lower when I do, when branded Ahab gives chase to Moby Dick. That hazard shall not be yours. No, no! not with the far-away home I see in that eye!"

items.new: "Oh, my Captain! my Captain! noble soul! grand old heart, after all! Why should anyone give chase to that hated fish? Away with me! Let us fly these deadly waters! Let us go home! Wife and child, too, are Starbuck's — wife and child of his brotherly, sisterly, play-fellow youth; just as yours, sir, are the wife and child of your loving, longing, paternal old age! Away! Let us away! — let me alter the course this instant! How cheerily, how hilariously, O my Captain, we would bowl along on our way to see old Nantucket again! I think, sir, they have some such mild blue days, just like this one, in Nantucket."

items.new: "What is it, what nameless, inscrutable, unearthly thing is it; what deceiving, hidden lord and master, and cruel, remorseless emperor commands me; that against all natural lovings and longings, I keep on pushing, and crowding, and jamming myself on like this all the time; recklessly making me ready to do what in my own proper, natural heart I would not so much as dare? Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm? But if the great sun does not move of himself, but is as an errand-boy in heaven; and not one single star can revolve except by some invisible power; how then can this one small heart beat, this one small brain think thoughts, unless God does that beating, does that thinking, does that living, and not I? By heaven, man, we are turned round and round in this world, like that windlass there, and Fate is the handspike. And all the while — there! — that smiling sky, and this unsounded sea! Look! see that Albicore there! Who put it into him to chase and fang that flying-fish? Where do murderers go, man? Who's to doom, when the judge himself is dragged to the bar? But it is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky; and the air smells now as if it blew from a far-away meadow; they have been making hay somewhere under the slopes of the Andes, Starbuck, and the mowers are sleeping among the new-mown hay. Sleeping? Aye, toil as we may, we all sleep at last on the field. Sleep? Aye, and rust amid greenness, like last year's scythes flung down and left in the half-cut swaths — Starbuck!"
